description: We gonna make an app for farmers :DDD
summary:
What the app does

Plan: it replays 29 past seasons on the field with the same crop, before and after. A new crop is labelled as a new planting, with where and when. This tests a plan against past weather. It is not a yield forecast.
Today: one clear action for the day, with weather in plain units (wind in m/s, soil in %, solar in kWh/m²/day).
Next season: a plan for the next planting, with a readable stress calendar.
Data connectors: a tab where every source and device has its own card with its status. Data shows only while its source is connected.
Map: NASA satellite layers, dry zones, and field and device icons, with the options grouped so they are less messy.
Dashboard: an optional full-screen view.
Add data: simple, with NASA data loading automatically.
details:
What it does. Ceresmind turns 30 years of NASA weather into one clear plan for a farmer’s field. The farmer marks a field and picks a crop. The app replays 29 past seasons of NASA POWER weather on that field, using a crop-growth and soil-water model. It then shows how often the field would have been too dry or too hot with today’s practice versus a better plan (timing and watering). Each day it gives one action, such as “water today”. It also plans next season, and any new crop is clearly labelled as a new planting with where and when. This is a test against past weather, not a yield forecast.

Benefits and impact. Small farms get decisions based on NASA data without an agronomist, an account or a server. In our demo farm the plan lifts the resilience score from 48 to 79 and cuts stress seasons from 31% to 9%, with about 14% more yield and water use down from 520 to 458 mm. These are example-farm figures, not field trials. The aim is that farmers adapt before the bad year, not after it.

How it works. NASA POWER gives 30 years of weather. NASA GIBS gives satellite layers, and NASA EONET gives events. Open-Meteo and ISRIC SoilGrids add live weather and soil. A Data connectors tab shows each source and device on its own card with its status, and data appears only while its source is connected. Optional sensors can be added over MQTT, REST, ThingSpeak or files.

Tools. The app is a single offline HTML file built from plain JavaScript modules. We used Leaflet for maps, SheetJS for spreadsheets, MQTT.js for devices and Playwright for testing. No install, account or hardware is required.

Creativity. The 30-year replay turns climate data into a plain “bad years” count. One screen and one action a day keep it usable for non-experts.

Factors considered. We kept it simple, with minimal words and consistent terms. It is honest about its limits, works offline, and its units are clear (m/s, % and kWh/m²/day).

AI use. Claude and Gemini helped draft code, slides and documents. Our team reviewed, merged and tested everything and answers for the claims.
dataRefs: NASA EONET (Earth Observatory Natural Event Tracker), fires, storms and floods
NASA GIBS (Global Imagery Browse Services), satellite map layers
NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), daily weather API
